newsitem.title: ITALY: Opposition protests against Italy austerity budget.
newsitem.headline: Opposition protests against Italy austerity budget.

text.p: Opposition parties staged protests across Italy on Sunday against the government's 1997 austerity budget, a day after the draft law was approved by the lower house of parliament.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi says the deficit-cutting package is vital if Italy is to become a founder member of planned European monetary and economic union (EMU).

As a big step towards reaching that goal, he said on Saturday his centre-left government would soon ask to put the lira back into the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM), four years after it crashed out of the grid in a currency crisis.
"From today, tomorrow or the day after we will start negotiations for the lira's return to the ERM," a smiling Prodi told reporters minutes after the lower house ratification.
While the main centre-right opposition bloc, led by Silvio Berlusconi, supports EMU, it has blasted the budget as recessionary and boycotted Saturday's vote.

Unions have also slammed the belt-tightening package, which is designed to strip a massive 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) from next year's projected public sector deficit through a mix of spending cuts and revenue-raising measures.

In an important test to see if the government's popularity has been soured by the budget, local elections involving one million voters were held on Sunday in town councils throughout Italy. First results were due on Monday.

To coincide with the polls, Berlusconi's Freedom Alliance bloc called for demonstrations against the budget in 100 cities, dubbing the event "a Sunday for Freedom," in a series of full page advertisements which appeared in weekend newspapers.
"We don't want to take any responsiblity for a budget which will prove ruinous for the country," Berlusconi told a packed rally in the northern city of Milan.

He said the Freedom Alliance would continue its budget boycott when the bill moved to the Senate next week. Under Italian law both houses of parliament must approve legislation before it passes to the statute book.
Prodi has to rely on the support of the hardline Communist Refoundation in the lower house but needs no outside backing in the Senate, which should ensure smooth passage for the law.

However the government could face trouble from trades unions, who have threatened to call a general strike over the budget's fiscal plans, which hit employees much more than the self-employed. They are also angry that financing for a recent labour accord has not been covered in the budget.

Prodi is due to meet union leaders on Monday to discuss their objections. "At the moment I think the chances of reaching an accord are less than 50 percent. The situation is critical," Pietro Larizza, leader of the UIL union, said at the weekend.

Prodi has promised to give the unions details of a one-off "Euro Tax', which is expected to rake in 12.5 trillion lire ($8.25 billion) next year and has proved one of the most controversial aspects of the budget law.

The Il Sole 24 Ore newspaper said at the weekend that the Finance Ministry was considering issuing privatisation bonds to offset the impact of the levy, which is expected to rely heavily on a hike in income tax.
The bonds would give taxpayers shares in various state firms when they are eventually sold off. ($1=1516 Lire)
